title: Job 31:13–23
context: Job continues his oath of clearance. In 31:13–23 he turns to how he treated those with little power: his male and female servants, the poor, the widow, the fatherless, and the needy without clothing. He grounds the servant’s claim to justice in a shared Creator (31:15), and he denies using his standing at the city gate against the vulnerable. These lines answer, point by point, the kind of accusations Eliphaz made in 22:6–9. The household arrangements reflect Job’s ancient world and are reported, not commended as a model; what both traditions draw from the passage is Job’s conviction that the weak have a real claim on the strong before God. Job’s description of his care for the poor echoes his memory of former days in 29:12–17.

verses.text: “If I have despised the cause of my male servant or of my female servant, when they contended with me,
verses.arminianNotes: Job disowns despising the cause of his male or female servant when they had a complaint against him. Arminian readers note that Job claims to have given those under his authority a real hearing and fair dealing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job acknowledging that his servants had a just claim he was bound to honor. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse carefully, reporting Job’s ancient household setting while drawing out the duty of justice to the weaker party.

verses.text: what then will I do when God rises up? When he visits, what will I answer him?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks what he will do when God rises up and visits, and what he could answer. Arminian readers see Job’s sense of accountability: he treated his servants fairly because he himself must answer to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job locates the ground of justice in God’s judgment, before whom master and servant alike must stand. Both traditions read the verse as Job’s reverent awareness that God takes up the cause of the lowly.

verses.text: Didn’t he who made me in the womb make him? Didn’t one fashion us in the womb?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks whether the one who made him in the womb did not also make his servant. Arminian readers see a striking claim of shared human dignity: master and servant alike are fashioned by the same Creator.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the verse grounding the servant’s worth in God’s creative work, not in social rank. Shared ground: both traditions treat 31:15 as a significant witness to the common humanity of all people before God.

verses.text: “If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail,
verses.arminianNotes: Job disowns withholding the poor from their desire or causing the widow’s eyes to fail with waiting. Arminian readers note that Job claims active care, not merely the avoidance of harm toward those in need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job answering the charge that he sent widows away empty (compare 22:9). Both traditions read the verse as Job’s claim that he responded to the needs of the poor and the widow rather than turning away.

verses.text: or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it
verses.arminianNotes: Job disowns eating his morsel alone while the fatherless went without. Arminian readers see the image of shared bread as everyday generosity, part of the righteous life Job says he chose to live.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job counts private self-indulgence, eating alone while others lack, as a real wrong. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an ethic of table fellowship that includes the orphan.

verses.text: (no, from my youth he grew up with me as with a father, I have guided her from my mother’s womb);
verses.arminianNotes: In a parenthesis Job says that from his youth the fatherless grew up with him as with a father, and he guided the widow from his mother’s womb. Arminian readers see a lifelong pattern of care, not a single act of charity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the hyperbole of from my mother’s womb, stressing that care for the vulnerable marked Job’s whole life. Both traditions read the parenthesis as Job’s claim that his concern for orphan and widow was longstanding.

verses.text: if I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or that the needy had no covering;
verses.arminianNotes: Job disowns seeing anyone perish for lack of clothing or the needy without covering. Arminian readers note that Job claims to have noticed the needy, as attention to others’ suffering is itself a moral act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job answering Eliphaz’s charge that he stripped the naked (compare 22:6). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job denying that he ignored the basic bodily needs of others.

verses.text: if his heart hasn’t blessed me, if he hasn’t been warmed with my sheep’s fleece;
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks whether the needy did not bless him when warmed by the fleece of his sheep. Arminian readers see the gratitude of those he helped as a witness to his conduct, testimony from the recipients themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the concrete detail: wool from Job’s own flock clothing the poor. Both traditions read the verse as Job pointing to tangible generosity that others could confirm, not to vague good intentions.

verses.text: if I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless, because I saw my help in the gate;
verses.arminianNotes: Job disowns raising his hand against the fatherless because he saw that he had support in the gate. Arminian readers note that the gate was the place of legal decision, where Job could have exploited his influence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as denying abuse of power in court, a sin the prophets also condemn. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as Job’s claim that he did not use his standing to crush the defenseless.

verses.text: then let my shoulder fall from the shoulder blade, and my arm be broken from the bone.
verses.arminianNotes: Job calls down a fitting penalty: let his shoulder fall from its blade and his arm be broken from the bone. Arminian readers see the arm that might have been raised against the orphan made the very object of the curse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the image answers Eliphaz’s claim that the arms of the fatherless had been broken (compare 22:9). Both traditions read the self-curse as matching the alleged crime, measure for measure.

verses.text: For calamity from God is a terror to me. Because of his majesty, I can do nothing.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says calamity from God is a terror to him, and before his majesty he can do nothing. Arminian readers see reverent fear as the motive behind his justice: he dealt rightly with others because he feared God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job’s conduct springs from awe at God’s majesty, the fear of the LORD the wisdom books commend. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as revealing the God-ward root of Job’s ethics.
